query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the as-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, the combination of low Al content with a high density of grain boundaries (inherited from rapid solidification) leads to preferential oxygen diffusion along defects. This results in an incomplete and spatially heterogeneous formation of protective oxide scales (with mostly chromia and intermittent, insufficient alumina), allowing internal oxidation and stress-driven phase destabilization (e.g., localized FCC to brittle BCC transformation) that ultimately causes catastrophic failure during high‐temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an ultrafine-grained FCC matrix exhibiting high defect and grain boundary density and only modest Al levels.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post‐fabrication heat treatment to coarsen the grain structure and thereby reduce the grain boundary density.
generation.conditions: Expose samples to elevated temperatures (850–1050 °C) under controlled oxidizing atmospheres (with defined oxygen partial pressures) as well as under reducing gas conditions to compare outcomes.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density governs the preferential pathways for oxygen diffusion and hence the efficacy and uniformity of oxide scale formation.
generation.mechanism: A high density of grain boundaries in the as-built state accelerates oxygen ingress leading to internal oxidation. With limited Al available to form a continuous protective alumina layer, the oxide layer becomes non-uniform and prone to spallation. Consequently, local depletion and stress concentration trigger a phase transformation from the ductile FCC to a brittle BCC phase, undermining the mechanical integrity and precipitating catastrophic failure under sustained thermal and chemical exposures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built (ultrafine-grained) baseline, heat-treated (coarsened-grain) samples will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics, more uniform and adherent oxide scales, reduced internal oxidation, and a delay or reduction in the onset of brittle phase transformation under oxidizing conditions. Under reducing conditions, while oxidation is minimized, the elimination of other degradation features will be evident in mechanical testing.
generation.baseline: The as-built additive manufactured state, which shows rapid oxidation, heterogeneous (spalling) oxide layer formation, and early transition to brittle phases at 900–1050 °C, correlating with catastrophic failure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-temperature exposures in the 850–1050 °C range, with specific gas environments characterized as either oxidizing (controlled oxygen partial pressure) or reducing.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings on oxidation kinetics and deformation mechanisms from studies in similar HEAs (e.g., evidence in PMC9026100 and PMC9969177) by linking them to additive manufacturing–specific microstructural features. The role of low Al content is extrapolated from conflicting reports (PMC11169556), and its exact impact in this alloy remains uncertain until tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one in the as-built ultrafine-grained state and the other subjected to a post-fabrication heat treatment designed to coarsen the grains (reducing grain boundary density). Expose both sets to 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 hours each under controlled oxidizing gas atmospheres (and separately under reducing conditions) while monitoring oxidation kinetics and phase evolution.
measurements: Mass gain measurements to quantify oxidation kinetics
High-resolution SEM/TEM imaging to assess oxide scale morphology and internal oxidation depth
XRD analysis to identify phase changes, particularly the emergence of BCC phases
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or creep tests) to determine ductility loss or catastrophic failure onset
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the grain-coarsened samples do not exhibit significantly improved oxidation behavior (i.e., reduced mass gain, more uniform and adherent oxide layers, and delayed or diminished brittle phase transformation and failure) relative to the as-built samples under oxidizing conditions, then the hypothesis that grain boundary–mediated internal oxidation governs degradation would be falsified.

AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
